claims.text: The proposed multiscale approach separately models phonon and electronic heat transport.
The proposed approach will predict the independent lattice and electronic thermal conductivities of HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than previous perfect-crystal methods.
The target material is single-phase HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The phonon calculation includes anharmonicity and defect- or impurity-induced scattering without relying on a single Debye-temperature approximation.
Electronic structure and electron-phonon coupling are calculated independently using DFT.
The model is intended to apply under equilibrium conditions from approximately 50 K to 1200 K.
Below 200 K, the lattice and electronic contributions to thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr are similar.
Between 300 K and 1200 K, the total thermal conductivity of the approximately 1 wt.% oxygen specimen is 10–17 W/(K·m).
Direct incorporation of atomic-scale disorder and oxygen impurities mediates their effects on phonon scattering.
Electronic transport can be evaluated independently from the impurity-perturbed band structure.
Atomic-mass variation, force-constant disorder, and impurity perturbations produce phonon scattering that the proposed approach treats explicitly.
Separating phonon and electronic channels avoids conflation in earlier models and better captures the complexity of real HfNbTaTiZr specimens.
Below 200 K, the model will predict nearly equal lattice and electronic thermal conductivities.
At higher temperatures, the lattice thermal-conductivity contribution will remain relatively steady.
At higher temperatures, the electronic thermal-conductivity contribution will decrease.
The combined high-temperature thermal conductivity will be 10–17 W/(K·m).
The new approach will reduce predictive error by approximately 20% relative to earlier analytical methods.
Earlier models used simplified Debye approximations or perfect-crystal DFT-derived properties and did not capture oxygen impurities or full atomic-scale disorder.

The prediction is limited to single-phase HfNbTaTiZr with approximately 1 wt.% oxygen between 50 K and 1200 K and may not remain robust at substantially different oxygen levels or after phase instability or segregation.
Local clustering or short-range order may modify scattering rates and thereby affect predictive accuracy.
